steps.title: Crude oil
steps.body: is a mixture of hydrocarbons that formed from the remains of ancient biomass (mostly plankton) over millions of years under high pressure and temperature. It is a finite resource — it cannot be replaced once used.

steps.title: Fractional distillation
steps.body: separates crude oil into fractions (groups of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points). The crude oil is heated and vapours rise up a fractionating column. Fractions condense at different heights depending on their boiling points .

steps.title: Key idea 3
steps.body: A hydrocarbon is a compound of carbon and hydrogen only . No other elements are present.

steps.title: Alkanes
steps.body: are saturated hydrocarbons — they contain only single carbon–carbon bonds . The general formula for alkanes is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ .

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: What is crude oil a mixture of? Explain why crude oil is described as a finite resource. | Describe how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions. Explain why fractions condense at different heights in the column. | An alkane has 5 carbon atoms. Use the general formula to work out its molecular formula and name it.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When asked about fractional distillation, always mention the temperature gradient (hot at bottom, cool at top) and that separation happens because different fractions have different boiling points When writing cracking equations, always check your carbon and hydrogen atoms balance on both sides Cracking always produces at least one alkene — this is a common exam point Bromine water test: decolourises = alkene (unsaturated); stays orange = alkane (saturated) Properties trend: longer chains → higher boiling point, more viscous, less flammable, less volatile
